prompt: Which HTTP method is idempotent but not safe?
options: PUT
GET
POST
PATCH
explanation: Safe means no server-side effect (GET, HEAD). Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once: PUT and DELETE. POST isn't idempotent, and PATCH isn't guaranteed to be ("increment by 1" is a valid patch).

prompt: An authenticated user calls an admin-only endpoint. What status code fits?
options: 403 Forbidden
401 Unauthorized
400 Bad Request
404 Not Found
explanation: 401 means "I don't know who you are": credentials are missing or invalid, and the response should include WWW-Authenticate. 403 means "I know who you are, and you're not allowed". Some APIs return 404 deliberately to hide that a resource exists, but that's a choice, not the default.

prompt: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection. What head-of-line blocking remains, and what fixes it?
options: TCP-level: one lost packet stalls all streams; HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes it
None: multiplexing over one connection removes all head-of-line blocking
Response-level: replies must return in order; pipelining fixes it
DNS-level: one slow lookup blocks every stream; DNS over HTTPS fixes it
explanation: HTTP/2 removed HTTP/1.1's in-order responses per connection, but TCP delivers bytes strictly in order, so a single loss blocks every stream. QUIC handles loss per stream and also merges the transport and TLS handshakes.

prompt: Two admins load the same order (ETag "v7") and each sends PUT /orders/42 with If-Match: "v7". The first PUT succeeds. What should the server return for the second PUT, and why?
options: 304 Not Modified, because the client's cached copy of the order is stale
409 Conflict, because two clients tried to write the same resource at once
412 Precondition Failed, because the ETag no longer matches "v7"
200 OK, because PUT is idempotent and the last write simply wins
explanation: If-Match makes the write conditional: the first PUT changed the ETag, so the second request's precondition is false and the server returns 412. The client re-fetches, merges, and retries. 304 belongs to conditional GETs (If-None-Match), not writes. Idempotent only means repeating the same request has the same effect. It doesn't stop a lost update.

prompt: What does the HttpOnly cookie attribute do?
options: Stops page JavaScript from reading the cookie via document.cookie
Sends the cookie only over HTTPS connections, never over plain HTTP
Blocks the cookie from being sent on any cross-site request at all
Deletes the cookie automatically as soon as the browser is closed
explanation: HTTPS-only is the Secure attribute, and cross-site behavior is SameSite. HttpOnly doesn't prevent XSS itself: injected script can still make requests that carry the cookie, it just can't steal it.

prompt: Why are JWT access tokens usually short-lived (around 5–15 minutes) and paired with refresh tokens?
options: Self-contained tokens can't easily be revoked, so expiry limits leaks
Browsers discard stored bearer tokens after about 15 minutes idle
The RS256 signature grows weaker the longer a token stays in use
JWT payloads are capped at 1 KB, so they must be refreshed often
explanation: Statelessness is the point of a JWT and also its weakness. Refresh tokens are stored server-side or rotated, so they can be revoked, and they mint new access tokens. Alternatives are opaque tokens with introspection, or a denylist keyed by jti.

prompt: A session cookie has SameSite=Lax. Which cross-site request still carries it?
options: A cross-site form POST to your endpoint
A top-level GET navigation from a link
An tag embedded on another site
A cross-site fetch() with credentials: 'include'
explanation: Lax sends cookies on top-level navigations that use safe methods, which is why a state-changing GET is still CSRF-able. Subresource requests and cross-site POSTs don't carry the cookie. Strict blocks even link navigations, so users arrive logged out.

prompt: You change a DNS A record, but some users reach the old IP for hours. Why?
options: Resolvers keep serving the cached record until its TTL expires
The registrar needs hours to approve every A-record change
DNS changes only take effect after the web server restarts
Browsers ignore DNS and reuse the last IP they connected to
explanation: TTL controls how long caches may keep a record. Lower the TTL well before a planned migration (at least one old-TTL period earlier), make the switch, then raise it again. Some resolvers also enforce their own minimum TTL.

prompt: On a new HTTPS connection (TCP + TLS 1.3, no session resumption), how many round trips happen before the client can send its first HTTP request?
explanation: One RTT for the TCP handshake and one for the TLS 1.3 handshake (TLS 1.2 needs two). That's why connection reuse, keep-alive and HTTP/3 (which combines both into one RTT, or zero with resumption) matter so much for latency.

prompt: How does traffic sent to a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service actually reach a pod?
options: kube-proxy rules on each node DNAT the virtual IP to a ready pod
A proxy process listens on the ClusterIP and forwards connections
CoreDNS returns a pod IP directly for every lookup of the Service
The Ingress controller receives and routes all Service traffic
explanation: The ClusterIP is virtual: nothing listens on it. The rules are rewritten from EndpointSlices, and only pods that pass their readiness probe are included. Headless Services (clusterIP: None) are the case where DNS returns pod IPs directly.

prompt: Who enforces CORS?
options: The browser, using the server's Access-Control-* response headers
The API server, which rejects any request from a disallowed origin
The load balancer, based on the Origin header of each request
The DNS resolver, which refuses lookups for foreign origins
explanation: CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy. It isn't server-side access control: curl and other servers ignore it entirely, and a simple request may still reach the server and run. Real authorization still has to happen on the server.

prompt: An Angular app calls an API on another origin with an Authorization header and Content-Type: application/json. What does the browser do first?
options: Sends it directly, since Angular's HttpClient handles CORS itself
Sends an OPTIONS preflight first, because it isn't a simple request
Blocks it outright, since Authorization is never sent cross-origin
Downgrades it to a simple GET without the custom request headers
explanation: Simple requests use only GET/HEAD/POST, CORS-safelisted headers, and form or text content types. Anything else triggers a preflight, and the server must answer with Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers. Access-Control-Max-Age caches the preflight result.

prompt: What is the difference between Cache-Control: no-cache and no-store?
options: no-cache may store but must revalidate; no-store must never store
They're synonyms that both disable caching in every cache layer
no-store lets CDNs cache but not browsers; no-cache does the reverse
no-cache disables ETags, while no-store disables Last-Modified checks
explanation: no-cache plus an ETag is the usual setup for index.html: the browser always checks, and an unchanged page costs only a cheap 304. no-store is for sensitive responses. Hashed static assets should use max-age=31536000, immutable.

prompt: What is an IP address used for?
options: Naming a web page for people to read
Identifying a computer so packets can find it
Encrypting a message before it is sent
Storing a user's password on a server
explanation: An IP address is the network address of a computer, like a street address for a building. Routers read it to forward each packet one step closer to its destination.

prompt: Why are messages sent over the internet split into packets?
options: Routers can only read tiny messages
It is required before data can be encrypted
A lost piece can be resent on its own
It makes each IP address unique to you
explanation: Small packets can take different routes and be retransmitted individually if one is lost. That makes delivery flexible and resilient, instead of all-or-nothing.

prompt: A server has one IP address but runs a web server and a mail server. How does incoming data reach the right program?
options: By the port number
By the packet's size
By the router's brand
By the time of day
explanation: The IP address finds the computer, and the port number picks which program on it receives the data. Web traffic normally uses port 443 or 80, while mail uses other ports.

prompt: What does TCP add on top of IP?
options: A friendly name for the server
Reliable, ordered delivery with resends
Faster routers across the whole network
A much longer address space for computers
explanation: IP only moves packets on a best-effort basis, so they can be lost or arrive out of order. TCP numbers them, acknowledges what arrived, resends what is missing and reassembles the data in order.

prompt: In https://shop.example.com/cart?id=7, what is /cart?
options: The scheme
The query
The path
The host
explanation: The path comes after the host and names the resource being requested. The query starts at the question mark and holds extra key=value options.

prompt: What does DNS do?
options: Maps a domain name to an IP address
Encrypts the traffic between you and a site
Hosts the web page files for a website
Blocks unwanted traffic from reaching you
explanation: DNS is the internet's lookup service for names. Your browser asks it for the IP address behind a name, and then connects to that address to get the page.

prompt: You change a DNS record's IP address, but some users still reach the old server for a while. Why?
options: The new server is slower than the old
Browsers never ask DNS for anything at all
Cached answers last until their TTL ends
IP addresses are not allowed to change ever
explanation: Resolvers, operating systems and browsers cache answers for the record's TTL. Until a cache's copy expires, it keeps returning the old address, so changes spread gradually.

prompt: Which part of a URL is never sent to the server?
options: The path of the page
The fragment after the hash sign
The query string with its options
The host name of the server itself
explanation: The fragment points to a spot inside the page and is handled only by the browser. The host is used for the connection, and the path and query are included in the request.

prompt: Which status code range means the client made a mistake?
options: 2xx
3xx
4xx
5xx
explanation: 4xx codes such as 400 and 404 say the request itself was the problem. 5xx codes say the server failed even though the request was fine.

prompt: Which part of an HTTP response comes after the blank line?
options: The body
The status line
The headers
The method
explanation: A blank line ends the headers, and everything after it is the body, such as the HTML or JSON. The status line comes first, then the headers.

prompt: A crawler visits thousands of pages using GET. Why must GET never change data?
options: GET bodies are always far too small to matter
GET is always slower than POST for this job
GET cannot carry any headers or a body at all
Anyone may repeat GET, so it must be harmless
explanation: GET is meant to be safe: browsers, caches and crawlers may call it any number of times. If it deleted or created something, ordinary page visits would cause damage.

prompt: What does the Content-Type header on a POST request tell the server?
options: How to read the body, e.g. JSON
Which server the client should connect to
How long to keep the connection open
Whether the user is currently logged in
explanation: The body is just bytes until a Content-Type labels it, for example application/json. The server uses that label to choose how to parse it.

prompt: Why does a website need cookies, sessions or tokens to keep you logged in?
options: Browsers forget the password you typed
HTTP requests are independent of each other
Servers can only ever talk to one user
Passwords expire after every single request
explanation: HTTP has no memory between requests. After login, the server gives the client something to send each time, so it can tell the requests belong to the same user.

prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication is about speed, not identity
They are simply two names for one thing
Authorization proves who you are, authentication sets limits
Authentication proves who you are; authorization sets limits
explanation: Authentication answers who you are, usually with a password. Authorization answers what you are allowed to do, and it must be checked on every action.

prompt: In a server-side session, what should the cookie contain?
options: A random session ID
The user's password
The user's full profile and permissions
The server's secret key
explanation: The cookie is only a lookup key, and the real data lives on the server. That keeps secrets away from the browser and lets the server end a session by deleting its record.

prompt: Why are signed tokens such as JWTs usually given a short lifetime?
options: Long tokens take far too much space to store safely
They are hard to revoke: no server record
The browser deletes every token it ever receives
Short tokens are always encrypted better than long ones
explanation: A signed token is accepted by anyone who checks its signature, with no lookup, so the server cannot easily revoke one. A short expiry limits how long a stolen token is useful.
